text:
In stark contrast to the hollow triumphalism and gilded monuments of the Core Worlds, the Blackcollar memorial bay on Crucible Base is vast, echoing, and dead silent. The air is bone-cold, smelling faintly of ancient ozone and chilled composite armor.
At the center of the pressurized cavern—carved directly out of the keel of the original exile sporeship—rises a monumental monolith of matte-black carbon-titanium. The lower third is dense with laser-etched micro-inscriptions. Every fallen soldier of the Legion is recorded in immutable, egalitarian succession: Service ID, Name, Casualty Date, System Vector. There is no distinction of rank, caste, or origin; no flowery eulogies or moral judgments. Overhead, optical laser scribes hum in near-imperceptible pulses, engraving the latest casualties into the stone with pitiless mechanical precision.
Two Legionaries in matte-black powered armor stand motionless vigil with mag-clamped rifles, unblinking as statuary. As your HUD interfaces with the memorial's optical index, thousands of amber names flicker across your vision. You depart in subdued silence, humbled by the weight of so much sacrifice recorded with such clinical, uncompromising honor.

Welcome to the forge, Captain. Out here in the Rose Nebula, our crews are working around the clock to keep our flotillas battle-ready against the Protectorate's iron grip. text:
You follow the faded yellow guide-stripes through the vibration-rattled utility tunnels of Rosebriar. The air grows dense, heavy with the scent of ozone, machine coolant, and the faint, sweet tang of dried desert petals.
As the passage widens into the cavernous central atrium, you are met with a breathtaking, sprawling monument to defiance. The entire aft bulkhead is a jagged mosaic of memory. Thousands of artificial poppies—woven from red and purple syn-silk—cascade down the reinforced steel walls, framing the personal relics of those who fell to the Protectorate's guns.

text:
You step closer to a cluster of physical artifacts illuminated by amber lumen-strips. A cracked worker's hardhat rests on a shattered riot shield, both deeply scored by kinetic impacts. Beside them lies a jury-rigged kinetic carbine—its barrel warped from overheating, its stock wrapped in blood-stained grip tape.
A small holo-cube next to the weapon projects the grainy image of a young engineer, her face smeared with grease, raising the very same rifle in defiance. It is a testament to the brutal, asymmetric reality of the First Uprising: shipyard tools turned against military-grade armor.

Pinned to the steel bulkhead with thick solder wire are hundreds of thermal flimsies. You lean in to read them. Many are radical manifestos demanding labor rights and an end to the Admiralty's martial law, their ink smeared by time and handling.
Others are desperately personal: last letters written to spouses left behind on Valca, poetry composed in the dark hours of a Protectorate siege, and crude sketches of a free Rosebriar. One crumpled note simply reads, "They can bomb the habitats, but they cannot bomb the hunger."

In the center of the shrine, a bank of cracked, mismatched CRT monitors plays a silent, endless loop of shaky helmet-cam footage.
You watch a grainy, black-and-white charge through a Magellan logistics depot. Partisans throw homemade thermite charges into the treads of Protectorate heavy mechs before being cut down in a hail of autocannon fire. The camera falls sideways, capturing a final, freezing frame of a Magellan boot stepping over the lens. It is a grim, unflinching reminder of the blood already spilled in the name of liberty.

You step back, taking in the full breadth of the memorial once more.
A group of off-duty dockers in patched, blast-scarred overalls stand nearby in hushed reverie. As you approach, one of them raises a battered tin cup toward the flickering screens. The first rebellion may have been drowned in fire by the Admiralty's boot, but this memorial does not mourn defeat. It smolders with the quiet, terrifying certainty that the second revolution is merely waiting for the spark.

text:
The vaulted guildhall is alive with the warmth of spacer solidarity. Around long communal benches, merchanter families, belter miners, and void-weathered haulers share steaming pans of spicy red crab stew and fresh bread baked from hydroponic grain. An old prospector with a battered acoustic instrument strikes up a chord, and within moments half the hall joins in with clinking tin mugs:
...There once was a ship that plied the stars,
And the name of the ship was the Lily of Mars,
The hyper storms ripped her up and down,
Take hold, ye spacers, take hold...
...Soon may the salvageman come,
To bring us drugs and organs and guns,
One day, when the scavenging’s done,
We’ll take our leave and go.
After a chorus of hearty void-ballads and countless invitations to stay for 'just one more draft!', you take your leave with a warmed spirit and the rare feeling of true kinship among the stars.
You've been around pirates, smugglers, and other types of criminals often enough, and know how to act so they see you as one of their own.
You've gained a measure of notoriety in the underworld of Magellan space, and know how to throw your weight around to get what you want.
You've proven useful to some of the leaders of the various criminal enterprises in the Sector. Harassing you is more trouble than it's worth.
Both your prowess in battle and your barbecue skills are legendary, and your connections and influence in the Magellan underworld, enviable.
The Herd, as a whole, only tend to view you with distrust. Incidentally, that's more than can be said for how they see fellow captains.
The Herd are generally only inhospitable towards you, which means you've already made a name for yourself as someone whose interests might align with theirs.
Your name is not known to Herd captains, for good or ill. Mostly ill, as they'll attack you without a second thought if the opportunity arises, although Herd bases will gladly trade with you.
